reasons: Only the imports and the bridge line labels were reviewed, about two of twelve sections.
The render tests draw this page, which gives some evidence it does not crash on real data.
I did not run these tests in this review.

terms.meaning: a table that walks from gross benefit down to the net result
the money unit, such as pounds, euros or Australian dollars
a range of low, base and high values for one figure
a band becoming tighter after a change in how it is calculated

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and the currency rule
sections.what: Brings in the data types, shared components, comparison helpers and formatters. The header says the page never totals across currencies.
sections.why: Stated in the header comment, which explains why the page exists in this form.
sections.watch_out: The imports must match the names in the bands module, or the page will not build.

sections.name: LINES
sections.title: Rows of the bridge
sections.what: Lists the four bridge lines in order: gross benefit, prerequisite cost, implementation cost and run cost, each with a plus or minus sign.
sections.why: The labels explain that the prerequisite cost is enabling work and the run cost is operating the estate for twelve months.
sections.watch_out: The signs are display labels only. This section does not check the data, so keep them matched to what the bridge data means.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 1)
sections.title: Headline duplication ratio and shared pools
sections.what: Shows the headline duplication ratio, which is the claimed effort divided by the deduplicated effort, next to those two totals. Below it, a table lists each shared capability pool with its claimants, the effort each one claimed, the pool counted once, the credited split, the build wave, and the stated basis for the split.
sections.why: Likely reason: the code comments say the ratio is the first number anyone questioning a total will want, so it is shown with the totals it is built from.
sections.watch_out: The pool is the largest single claim on it, not the sum of the claims, so changing that rule would change the ratio silently.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 2)
sections.title: Credited effort and split basis per pool
sections.what: Fills in each row of the pool table. It lists each claimant's credited effort and weight, then shows the reconciler's stated basis and a link to its evidence. If no attribution was recorded for a pool, it shows a red warning that the weights cannot be checked.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The comments say the weights drive the duplication ratio, so their basis must be visible beside them.
sections.watch_out: A pool with no evidence still shows its split. The note there says the split is a judgement, and that note is the only signal the reader gets.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 3)
sections.title: Band widths against the superseded contract
sections.what: Explains that the narrower uncertainty bands come from removing an old confidence penalty, not from new information. A table compares each process's band under the current and previous contract, and rows that did not change are marked.
sections.why: The section note says the reader most likely to be misled is someone comparing this run with last quarter's deliverable, so the difference is stated openly.
sections.watch_out: The explanatory note is cut off in the source file at the point where the reason is given, so the full wording of that reason could not be read here.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 4)
sections.title: Evidence standing of the value and by wave
sections.what: Shows the share of realised value that is backed by evidence, then a per-wave table. A wave with no evidence is flagged with a warning. A sentence saying narrowing followed evidence is shown only when the data supports it, otherwise a warning appears instead.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page is meant to show when a narrowing is a correction and when it is not, so the claim is computed from the rows instead of written in as fixed text.
sections.watch_out: The check that decides whether the sentence appears is the only thing keeping the claim honest, so changing it changes what the reader is told.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 5)
sections.title: The bridge from benefit to net benefit
sections.what: Draws one table per currency. Each table walks from benefit through the cost lines to a net benefit, with base, low and high columns. The low case pairs low benefit with high cost.
sections.why: The section note explains the pairing: an optimistic benefit paired with an optimistic cost would just repeat the base case under another name.
sections.watch_out: Each currency is its own table. Values from different currencies must never be added together on this page.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 6)
sections.title: Currency and run-cost warnings
sections.what: If the run has more than one currency, a banner states that no portfolio total is shown and gives the engine's stated reason. If it has one currency, a note says the bridge is the portfolio figure. A separate warning appears when any bridge has unpriced run cost, which means every net figure is too high by that amount.
sections.why: The comments explain that the conditional exists because a fixed message would contradict single-currency runs.
sections.watch_out: The engine's reason is shown word for word, so the page cannot disagree with the stored output about why no total exists.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 7)
sections.title: Prerequisite build cost per prerequisite
sections.what: Shows one row for each prerequisite: its kind, the wave it is built in, its build effort, its cost split by claimant weight, the claimants, and the evidence behind it.
sections.why: The section note says the figures come from the prerequisite assumptions and that this cost was added because prerequisites used to cost nothing.
sections.watch_out: Cost per currency is shown as separate lines, so a reader must check each currency separately.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 8)
sections.title: Twelve month run cost by component
sections.what: Lists the five run cost components per currency with a total. The total is computed on the page from those five parts and compared with the figure used in the bridge. A red divergence note appears if they differ by more than a tenth of a unit.
sections.why: The comments say the list of five is written by hand in two places, so this check catches a sixth component the engine adds later.
sections.watch_out: If the engine adds a component, this table will not show it, and the divergence note is the only sign something is missing.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 9)
sections.title: Reconciliation to the client's own figures
sections.what: Shows the basis for the baseline tie and a warning when a currency is shared by several engagements. A table lists each engagement's share of revenue and earnings, and flags any engagement whose net exceeds its stated earnings as implausible.
sections.why: The comments say the engine reports a shared currency's whole net, because splitting it per client is an allocation choice rather than arithmetic.
sections.watch_out: Do not add the engagement rows up. The same figure can appear more than once, so each share is only an upper bound.

sections.name: Portfolio (part 10)
sections.title: Sensitivity and assumptions
sections.what: The sensitivity table shows what the net benefit becomes when each parameter is moved to its low or high end, with the swing. The assumptions list shows every constant the bridge uses, with its value and basis.
sections.why: The section notes say the sensitivity table shows which assumption a client should check first, and that a number without its assumptions cannot be defended.
sections.watch_out: Each sensitivity row moves one parameter alone, so the rows do not add up to a combined range.

summary: The portfolio page, which shows the money bridge for each currency separately and states that no grand total exists.
purpose: Lets a reader compare the benefit and cost of each process without any adding up across currencies.
why: The header says an earlier version summed several currencies into one wrong number, and the engine refuses to do that, so the page must say so where a total would normally sit.
how: Reads the bridges and processes, lays out each bridge line, shows the band comparison, and adds warnings about narrowing. Uses the evidence index and the confidence helpers. Only the top of the file was reviewed here.
inputs: The artifacts with the value and process data, and the evidence index.
outputs: The portfolio page as drawn HTML.
risks: Adding amounts from different currencies would be a serious error. Only two of the twelve sections were reviewed, so the rest of the file is unchecked.
debug: If a total appears across currencies, check how the bridges are grouped. If a row shows another row's figure, check the column order in the band table. If the page is blank, check the render tests.
